PHANTOM // README02 // THE MISSION

02 / THE MISSION

Field-first. Built for the rack.

The technician in the aisle is the primary user. Everything else is secondary.

PHANTOM is an edge-execution tool for Data Center Technicians operating in Day 0 — the deployment phase, when racks are arriving, optics are getting seated, and the difference between a clean build and a three-day blocker is how fast the technician at the rack face can get answers. It is not a project-management tool. It is not a ticketing system. It is a field instrument, purpose-built for the person standing in front of a rack with gloves on.

FIELD vs. DESK

Most data center tooling is built for the desk — velocity estimates, burn-down charts, completion ETAs. PHANTOM covers the other half: the technician in the aisle, gloves on, headlamp bobbing, answering one question right now — what do I do with the piece of hardware in front of me?

SCOPE BOUNDARY — DAY 0 ONLY

Day 0 is deployment — new hardware, empty racks, the Engineering Design Plan as source of truth. Day 2 is operations — incidents, tickets, corporate documentation. PHANTOM is scoped to Day 0. Sixteen months and 591 shipped versions later, that boundary has never moved. The boundary is the product.

THE REFERENCE USER

A CoreWeave DCT, six hours into an eight-hour shift, in front of a GB300 NVL72. Gloves on. No cell signal. One free hand at best. Every feature is evaluated against that person in that moment. If it does not help them, it does not ship — and if a shipped feature stops helping them, it is retired.

ONE SITE BECAME MANY

PHANTOM began hard-wired to AUS-01. It now runs on per-site Master files with a single-resident policy — one Master loaded at a time, explicit eviction, provenance visible on every surface. The same instrument travels: Austin, Atlanta, Dallas, wherever the racks land next.

Three moves, total: load Master → pick rack → work the rack.
Everything a rack needs lives on that rack's screen. Nothing else earns a door.
THE MISSIONPHANTOM // 2026 // README // 2 / 15
PHANTOM // README03 // THE COST

03 / THE COST

What the gap costs, before what it builds.

The problem is structural, not local. It recurs at every site, at every shift change.

Day 0 deployment has no standard field artifact. A technician arriving on shift reconstructs context from memory, paper, chat threads, and whoever is still on the floor. That reconstruction is unbilled, unmeasured, and repeated at every handoff at every site. PHANTOM exists because that cost is systemic — it is not a problem with any one technician, any one site, or any one shift.

THE RECURRING LOSS MEASURED PER SITE

The magnitude varies — by site, crew size, deployment phase, and how much of the outgoing shift is still on the floor. A single universal figure would be false precision, and this document does not offer one. What does not vary is the structure: the reconstruction happens at every shift change, at every site, and none of it is captured anywhere. The pilot’s job is to measure it at one site under real conditions, not to defend a number estimated in advance.

THE DOWNSTREAM COST

Reconstructed context is lossy. A blocker known to the outgoing shift and not to the incoming one is rediscovered at the rack face — the three-day blocker that a five-minute note would have prevented. As-built accuracy carries the same exposure: what was actually verified, versus what was assumed, becomes unrecoverable once the crew rotates.

WHY EXISTING TOOLING DOES NOT CLOSE IT

Project-management and ticketing systems model the deployment from the desk, at day and week granularity, assuming a network and a keyboard. The gap is at rack granularity, in minutes, with gloves on and no signal. The desk tools are not wrong — they are aimed at a different question. Nothing currently in the stack owns the technician’s question.

WHAT A STANDARD WOULD CHANGE

A shift that ends with a generated, actor-credited artifact rather than a verbal handoff changes three things: the next technician starts from evidence instead of recall; the as-built record becomes a byproduct of the work rather than a separate task; and deployment status traces to measured state rather than to whoever was asked. The instrument is downstream of the standard. The standard is the contribution.

The claim this document makes: the artifact gap is the cost, and it reproduces across sites.
The pilot exists to measure it — at one site, under real conditions, before any figure is claimed.

PHANTOM // README04 // THE DOCTRINE

04 / THE DOCTRINE

Four laws. Every feature. No exceptions.

The Cold Aisle Filter grew teeth. What began as three gates is now a body of law.

LAW 1 — COLD HANDS, ZERO BARS

Does it help a gloved technician with no signal deploy hardware faster? 44pt tap targets. Offline core. Features that require network during field work do not pass. The AI assistant declares itself dimmed when there's no signal — it never pretends.

LAW 2 — DATA HONESTY

Displayed state may never outrank measured state. No synthetic telemetry, no invented baselines, no decorative percentages. A count that can't be traced to the Master is a defect. A claim cannot outrank a mismatch: a scan that contradicts the plan records FAIL even if the tech taps PASS.

LAW 3 — ONE DOOR PER FACT

Two paths to the same fact is a defect. A ship that opens a door must close at least one. Every spec carries a before/after door ledger. The app got smaller in navigation while it grew in capability — that is the point.

LAW 4 — EVERY LINE CREDITS THE ACTOR

No anonymous evidence. Every scan, note, photo, and phase transition carries an operator identity and timestamp in an append-only audit trail, immutable after sign-off. The record is the technician's proof of work.

RETIRED BY THE FILTER THE LAW IS ENFORCED

The filter runs against shipped code, not just proposals. Recent kills:

✕ The entire legacy UI house — ?legacy=1, its markup, CSS, and tokens. Deleted, not hidden.
✕ Synthetic GPU telemetry generator feeding hardcoded values. Found by graph audit. Removed.
✕ "Typical: 60 min" phase baselines — hardcoded, not measured. Now reads "no baseline yet."
✕ The 25% Shift Readiness score — decorative math. Readiness is a gate or a number, never a score.
✕ A "SYNCED" label that only meant "online." Relabeled to what it actually knows.
✕ TODAY Pulse, Crash Cart, duplicate tool grids — thousands of lines of desk furniture, deleted.

PHANTOM // README05 // THE SPINE

05 / THE SPINE

A shift has three acts.

Not three tabs. Three acts in time. The whole app is organized around how a shift actually runs.

01

RUN THE SHIFT

Arrive, load the Master, see the site. The first screen has one job: hand the technician a rack. No Master loaded means one sentence and one button. A Master loaded means "N racks on this site — tap one." A brand-new technician cannot make a wrong move because there is only one move.

02

WORK THE RACK

The rack is the unit of work — where the entire shift is spent. One tap opens everything that rack needs: five phases and their checks, devices with U positions, scan, photo, note, blocker, and rack-scoped tools like ISOLATE that appear only when the rack's state warrants them. Tools are actions, never destinations. The next check sits at the top with a verb.

03

CLOSE THE LOOP

The technician decides when to close out — never a timer, never a threshold. The handoff assembles itself from the work already logged: completed, carry forward, next shift starts here. A first shift ends with a legitimate artifact and the technician's name on every line of it.

The acts run in time, not space. Act 2 is where the shift lives.
Every queued ship is assigned an act, and must state how it makes that act shorter — measured in taps or screens.
Re-entry is always allowed. Closing the loop is a choice, not a gate slammed shut.
THE SPINEPHANTOM // 2026 // README // 5 / 15
PHANTOM // README06 // THE ARCHITECTURE

06 / THE ARCHITECTURE

Deliberate constraints. Each one explained.

Non-standard choices, documented so future contributors understand the constraint before they touch it.

ONE FILE — NO BUILD STEP

No NPM, no bundler, no compiler. The source in the repository is the source in the browser. A build step is a failure mode between the developer and the field technician; that surface is eliminated by design. One vendored library (ZXing, same-origin). No runtime CDN loads. The service worker caches the whole application; subsequent loads need no network.

DEVICE-LOCAL STORAGE — localStorage + IndexedDB

Network is unreliable in the cold aisle; on-device storage is always there. Deployments, audit trail, handoffs, and the Optic Ledger live in localStorage; photo evidence lives in IndexedDB where the byte budget belongs. Backup is explicit export. Restore is undoable by design — a snapshot is taken before applying, one-tap revert, and the restore refuses to run if the snapshot cannot be taken.

CLOUDFLARE WORKER — THE ONE EXCEPTION

Exactly one outbound path. The Worker holds the Anthropic API key as an encrypted secret — workspace-scoped, origin-locked to the app's exact URLs, POST-only, rate-capped via KV. Not a backend: a key-holder and origin filter. Every AI call is opt-in by user action.

TWO BRANCHES, ONE TRUTH

The phone is served from a release branch that only the owner promotes. main builds to a staging Worker where every ship is verified before graduation. Version lockstep is three-stamped (dct-ios.html / sw.js / version.json) and a pre-commit guard refuses version bumps that lack an owner-verified stamp. The pipeline cannot quietly ship what nobody checked.

Update path: git push → staging in seconds → verify on device → stamp → promote → phone pill reads the new build.
Rollback: git revert + cache bump. No app store, no MDM, no per-seat license. Cost of distribution: $0.
THE ARCHITECTUREPHANTOM // 2026 // README // 6 / 15

PHANTOM // README08 // DATA FLOW & SECURITY

08 / DATA FLOW & SECURITY

Where the data lives. Where it goes. Where it doesn't.

Device-local by default. Network by explicit action only. No telemetry vendor, no third-party analytics.

INPUTS
EDP paste design plan, text
BOM file CSV / xlsx
Scanner ZXing, on-device
Camera photo evidence
AI prompts user-initiated
→
PHANTOM CORE — ON-DEVICE
Deterministic parser SHA-256 cache · zero API calls
Rack state machine deployment → racks → phases → audit
localStorage + IndexedDB per-origin · OS-backed · offline
RBAC + mutation lock PIN-gated · immutable after sign-off
→
OUTPUTS
Audit trail append-only
Field report self-contained, generated
Handoff bundle tech to tech
JSON backup explicit export only
THE AI PATH — NETWORK-DEPENDENT, OPT-IN

App → Cloudflare Worker proxy → Anthropic API. The key lives as an encrypted Worker secret, workspace-scoped, never on device. Origin allowlist, POST-only, KV-capped. Streaming pass-through. Upstream errors logged to Cloudflare Observability — the app surfaces the real error, never a fabricated one.

A SECURITY CLAIM, EARNED THE HARD WAY

An earlier build carried a hardcoded API key in a secondary surface. It was found, revoked, and the entire path rebuilt: new workspace-scoped secret, proxy cutover verified from the live release — zero key strings client-side, zero direct API calls, all call sites on the Worker. The invariant "no keys live client-side" is now a verified property of the shipped code, not an aspiration. That is the difference between a security page and a security posture.

SHA-256 hashed PINs · 5-strike lockout · sign-off locks mutation · orphan records rejected on import
No persistent server-side storage of queries or responses · export is a human action, never a background sync

PHANTOM // README09 // THE SHIP DISCIPLINE

09 / THE SHIP DISCIPLINE

A process that catches its own lies.

The app is one file. The machine that ships it is the other half of the system.

PHANTOM ships one visible change at a time, and nothing reaches a technician's phone without surviving the gauntlet. This page did not exist in the May README because the gauntlet did not exist. It is the biggest thing built since.

ANCHORED PATCHES

Every patch is written against verified source via a knowledge graph of the live codebase, rebuilt before work begins. Assumed anchors are forbidden — a patch that cannot find its exact target stops and reports instead of improvising.

SEVEN REVIEW AGENTS

Specialist reviewers run on every change: lockstep audit, surgical-edit review, data-honesty audit, cold-aisle QA, storage archaeology, adapter review, report fidelity. Agent approval never substitutes for the owner's device check.

AUTOMATED E2E — REAL PHONE CONDITIONS

Playwright suites run against iPhone WebKit emulation as a precheck before any human verify. Known-broken behaviors are pinned with owner-ruled reasons, so a "pass" means something.

ADVERSARIAL MASTERS

Purpose-built torture fixtures — a 60-rack Master with 20 flagged, and a 29-trap CRUCIBLE with a seeded generator and trap manifest — exercise the app against hostile data before real sites ever do.

VERIFY → STAMP → PROMOTE — OWNER-ONLY

Every version is verified on a physical iPhone against staging. A VERIFIED stamp is committed from the owner's own terminal — no agent may issue one. Promotion to the served release branch is a separate owner-only act, guarded by a script that refuses unstamped or mismatched versions. Failed checks are recorded as FAILED, permanently. The register never forgets.

One visible change per ship. Batches of 3–5 run under a standing OODA loop; the owner gates the batch, never rubber-stamps the pile.
On one recorded day: 24 versions shipped, each device-verified. Discipline is not slow. Unverified is slow — it just bills you later.
THE SHIP DISCIPLINEPHANTOM // 2026 // README // 9 / 15
PHANTOM // README10 // THE HONESTY LEDGER

10 / THE HONESTY LEDGER

A field tool that can't tell you when it's guessing is asking for blind faith.

Data honesty is a trust primitive. These are real defects, found and executed — in public.

THE LIETHE TRUTHVERDICT
A telemetry function generating synthetic GPU values, rendered as if measuredPHANTOM has no live telemetry source. It now shows none.EXECUTED
"Typical: 60 min" phase baselines from a hardcoded tableNo history means no baseline. Reads "no baseline yet" until real logged data exists.EXECUTED
A readiness score of 25% computed from nothing actionableReadiness is a gate that answers or a number that traces. Scores are deleted.EXECUTED
"SYNCED" label on a device with no sync capabilityIt meant "online with no pending writes." It now says what it knows.EXECUTED
Blocker and rack counts rendered before any deployment existsNo active deployment → the cell reads not-applicable, never a counted zero.EXECUTED
Two engines counting one concept — hero and KPI cell disagreeing on rack countOne counting engine. Any two surfaces showing the same fact show the same number.EXECUTED
A rack reading "100% · done" while its log shows a bypassed validation gateUnder reconciliation now: may a bypassed phase ever render identical to a genuinely complete one? Recommendation on record: never.ON TRIAL
As-built exports marked VERIFIED without scope checks; missing BOM shown as definite shortageConfirmed by independent external review. Queued ahead of the field demo.ON TRIAL
The standing rule: displayed state never outranks measured state. If the app doesn't know, the app says so.
Every reference the field report makes carries a coverage manifest — what was checked, what wasn't, and who says so.

PHANTOM // README12 // ON THE TABLE

12 / ON THE TABLE

What's left, stated plainly.

A document that only shows the wins is a brochure. This is the open ledger.

FIELD VALIDATION — STILL THE GATE

The cover said "Field Validation Pending" in May and it still does. Hundreds of versions of hardening later, the pilot has not run — deliberately: the sandbox gates (navigation, data reconciliation, sync question) come first. The upcoming field demonstration is the event that finally changes the cover.

THE STRANGER TEST — CURRENTLY A 4 OF 10

Honest self-score for a technician who has never opened the app: 4. The first screen now answers "what do I do," and the rack surface is strong — but duplicate doors remain, one tool name collides with another, and close-out produces a flag instead of an artifact. The queued ships are, in order, the scoring path: one-door closures are worth two points on their own; the report is what makes a first shift make sense unaided.

ONE PHONE, ONE TRUTH — FOR NOW

All rack state is device-local today. Two technicians on one site cannot yet see each other's work. The sync architecture is fully specified — server-distributed Master, append-only actor-credited events, blocker-wins conflicts, offline queue — and deliberately parked until the single-phone experience earns it.

KNOWN DEFECT FAMILIES, PRIORITIZED

Confirmed by independent external review and owned: as-built exports need scope checks before claiming VERIFIED; missing BOM data must render as unknown, not shortage; service-worker install must never displace a working offline release with a failed one. First two are prioritized ahead of the demo. Nothing on this list is hidden from the roadmap — that would violate Law 2.

Standing verdict on rebuilds: rejected on principle. Punch-list ships only. The machinery exists to harden what works.
Day 2 remains out of scope. Sixteen months of pressure, zero drift. The boundary is the product.
THE TARGET STATE — TAP IT YOURSELF

Chapter 14 puts that shape in your hands as an interactive concept: every screen can be tapped, every job, rack and part in it is example data, and it was built outside the application rather than taken from it. The live application is being reorganized to that shape one verified ship at a time.

ON THE TABLEPHANTOM // 2026 // README // 12 / 15
PHANTOM // README13 // ADOPTION

13 / ADOPTION

What it takes to run this anywhere else.

Stated plainly, including what is not solved.

A tool only its author can operate is a personal productivity gain. A tool another site can adopt is a standard. This chapter states the difference honestly: what adoption requires today, what it does not yet support, and what would have to be true for PHANTOM to be owned by someone other than the person who wrote it.

WHAT ADOPTION COSTS TODAY

Distribution is a URL — no app store, no MDM, no per-seat license, zero marginal cost per technician. Onboarding a site requires one Master file for that site and nothing else. The blocker is not deployment cost; it is the stranger test scored in chapter twelve. Until that score rises, adoption is gated on navigation, not infrastructure.

WHAT IT DOES NOT YET SUPPORT

All state is device-local. Two technicians on one site cannot see each other’s work, and there is no cross-device transfer beyond an explicit export. The multi-technician architecture is specified and deliberately parked. A site adopting PHANTOM today adopts a single-phone instrument — stated here so that no adopter discovers it in an aisle.

THE OWNERSHIP QUESTION — UNRESOLVED

PHANTOM has one developer, who also holds a full deployment role. That is a concentration risk, and documentation alone does not solve it. The honest options: remain a field instrument owned by its author with no organizational dependency; be adopted by an enablement or tooling function with a maintainer assigned; or contribute its doctrine — the Cold Aisle Filter, the honesty ledger, the door law, the three-act spine — to whatever tool the organization does own. All three are legitimate. The decision is not the author’s to make alone.

WHAT TRANSFERS INDEPENDENT OF THE CODE

The reusable output is not the HTML file. It is the field-instrument standard: the reference-user test, displayed state never outranking measured state, one door per fact, the shift as three acts, evidence credited to an actor, and a published ledger of the tool’s own defects. Those apply to any Day 0 field tool, built by anyone, in any stack.

WHAT IS BEING ASKED

A scoped field pilot at one site: measured context-reconstruction time before and after, a stranger test run with a technician who has never opened the app, and a decision point at its conclusion on which of the three ownership paths the organization wants. Not a commitment to the tool — a commitment to measuring the gap.
